title: How Menstruation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain menstruation: the average cycle and its roughly four-week length, why humans and a few other mammals menstruate while most mammals undergo estrus, the ovarian and menstrual cycles (proliferative, follicular, ovulation, secretory, luteal phases), PMS and PMDD, the prostaglandin-driven shedding of the endometrium, and menstrual disorders (dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, menorrhagia). They then cover period products (cloths, reusable pads, disposable pads, tampons, menstrual cups and discs, costs), toxic shock syndrome and FDA regulation of tampons, cultural taboos and period poverty, myths (menstrual synchrony, not getting pregnant on your period, bears and sharks), a tampon shortage, and a listener mail water-safety note from former lifeguard Ella Fineberg about water wings and not attempting rescues while untrained.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: The hosts open, note they will use inclusive terms like girls, women and people who menstruate, and introduce menarche and the basic idea that menstruation happens about every four weeks.

segments.title: Why humans menstruate
segments.summary: Average cycle length and lifetime cycle count, the endometrium shedding, and why menstruation is rare among mammals (primates, elephant shrew, spiny mouse, vampire bat) versus estrus in most mammals, including sex-triggered ovulation. Discusses energy costs and malnutrition or athletic training suppressing periods, and discarded theories such as washing out pathogens and uterus size.

segments.title: Ovarian and menstrual cycle phases
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ovarian and menstrual cycles as two linked cycles: the proliferative phase with estradiol thickening the endometrium, the follicular phase with follicle stimulating hormone, the secretory phase, ovulation lasting about 24 hours, fertilization and ectopic pregnancy, and the luteal phase.

segments.title: Progesterone drop, PMS and shedding
segments.summary: Without fertilization, progesterone drops, causing PMS and PMDD, and prostaglandin constricts spiral arteries so the endometrium sheds as menstrual blood. The hosts note shedding prevents buildup and that intact endometrial casts can occur.

segments.title: Menstrual disorders: cramps, amenorrhea, menorrhagia
segments.summary: Overview of dysmenorrhea (cramps), primary and secondary amenorrhea and their causes, and menorrhagia (heavy flow), including when to see a doctor based on pad or tampon soaking.

segments.title: Period products and costs
segments.summary: Discussion of menstrual cloths and reusable pads, disposable pads and tampons, and menstrual cups and discs, with lifetime cost estimates and the pink tax, plus historical materials such as wool, grasses and ferns.

segments.title: Toxic shock syndrome and FDA regulation of tampons
segments.summary: Toxic shock syndrome from leaving tampons in too long, its symptoms, the proprietary ingredients issue, FDA regulation of tampons as medical devices, and advice on changing tampons and avoiding over-absorbent ones.

segments.title: Menstrual taboos and period poverty
segments.summary: Cultural taboos including the !Kung-style meal separation mentioned as the Koi people, European restrictions in the late 1800s, practices in Ghana and among the Ojibwe, and period poverty with charities that provide sanitary products.

segments.title: Menstrual myths
segments.summary: Myths debunked or unproven: menstrual synchrony (McClintock effect, 1971 study), pregnancy cannot occur on your period (sperm viability up to five days), and bears and sharks, including a National Park Service note that polar bears may be attracted to menstrual blood. Also a note on sexually transmitted infections during periods.

segments.title: Tampon shortage
segments.summary: Brief mention of a tampon shortage and a Tampax ad campaign featuring Amy Schumer that the company said boosted sales.

segments.title: Listener mail: water safety from Ella Fineberg
segments.summary: A former lifeguard writes about water wings not being safe flotation devices and advises against rescuing a drowning person without strong swimming ability; she recommends calling emergency services.
